summary:
GRAZE (ARTEMIS-VIEW) is an advanced lunar south pole mission planning and horizon navigation web application designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

What we developed: An intuitive flight console featuring a real-time 360-degree local horizon raycasting engine, side-by-side site comparison matrices, an interactive launch-slip shock-test simulator, and a scrubbable 30-day operational timeline.

How it addresses the challenge: By integrating NASA LOLA topographical data with topocentric ephemeris calculations, GRAZE visualizes exact Sun and Earth positions relative to jagged crater silhouettes. It dynamically computes solar power generation efficiency—factoring in mast height adjustments and panel orientations—while tracking Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication visibility.

Why it is important: Lunar south pole operations face extreme environmental constraints where a 500-meter coordinate shift or a minor launch date delay can plunge a lander into multi-day shadow blackouts and communication failure. GRAZE bridges the gap between raw scientific telemetry and rapid scenario evaluation, empowering engineers and planners to make agile, life-or-death mission decisions.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

GRAZE is an interactive lunar south pole mission planning and horizon navigation web application. It bridges the gap between complex orbital mechanics and rapid mission decision-making.

  • How it works:
    1. Topographic Horizon Raycasting: It utilizes pre-computed 360-degree terrain elevation profiles derived from NASA LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) high-resolution digital elevation models. For any selected landing site, it accounts for lunar spherical curvature and local crater/mountain ridges.
    2. Topocentric Ephemeris Engine: It computes the precise topocentric azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth in real time, accounting for the Moon's extreme $1.54^\circ$ axial tilt, the synodic solar cycle, and Earth's optical libration (the wobbling figure-8 path Earth traces in the lunar sky).
    3. Interactive Visualizations: It renders a 360° sky-dome panorama, a side-by-side site comparison matrix, a launch-slip shock-test simulator, and a scrubbable 30-day operational timeline tracking sunlight, Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows, and optimal overlap periods.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Rapid Scenario Evaluation: Instead of navigating cumbersome enterprise tools like NASA's Quickmap or JPL Horizons separately, planners can evaluate alternative sites or delayed launch dates in seconds.
  • Precision Risk Mitigation: It prevents catastrophic mission failures by accurately predicting multi-day shadow blackouts and communication dropouts caused by towering crater rims.
  • Hardware Trade-off Analysis: Features like the dynamic Solar Mast Height Adjuster (1m rover vs. 10m tower) let engineers instantly test how raising an array clears an obstructing ridge.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • For Mission Planners & Engineers: Accelerates coordination between science and engineering teams during NASA CLPS or commercial lunar missions, allowing rapid adaptation when launch delays or hardware changes force site re-evaluations.
  • For Education & Outreach: Serves as an engaging public-facing and educational tool that makes the harsh engineering realities of lunar south pole exploration—such as extreme shadowing and libration—instantly intuitive.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Core Framework & UI: React, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons.
  • Visualizations & Graphics: HTML5 Canvas and SVG for procedural shadow rendering, interactive 360° horizon panoramas, and responsive layout styling.
  • Data & Astronomy: Selenographic ephemeris calculation modules and curated topographic elevation profiles derived from NASA PGDA / LOLA datasets.
  • Version Control & Hosting: Git, GitHub (ARTEMIS-VIEW repository), and Vercel for instantaneous cloud deployment.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Interactive Hero Simulation: The landing page features an HTML5 canvas where moving the cursor sweeps the Sun's azimuth at a grazing $1.54^\circ$ elevation, casting real-time procedural shadow cones across Shackleton Crater while highlighting elevated ridges in golden light.
  • Scrollytelling Physics Briefing: Instead of static text, the app breaks down complex concepts (axial tilt, horizon occlusion, and Earth libration) through interactive, step-by-step visual cards.
  • High-End Flight Console Aesthetic: Abandoning generic tech styling, it adopts a custom design system ("Selenographic Obsidian & Regolith") featuring frosted basalt glassmorphism, vacuum black foundations (#050608), and tabular telemetry numerals.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Airless Vacuum Physics: Factoring in the total lack of atmospheric refraction, meaning terrain silhouettes dictate the horizon with razor-sharp precision and zero diffuse scattering.
  • Spherical Curvature & Scale: Ensuring long-baseline raycasting accurately accounted for the Moon's rapid horizon drop-off ($R = 1737.4\text{ km}$).
  • User Cognitive Load: Designing a single-screen command view that packs map navigation, sky-dome panoramas, timeline scrubs, and feasibility scorecards into a cohesive, jitter-free interface.
